description: Como el hornero que levanta su nido barro a barro en nuestra tierra, moldeamos software con la misma precisión, fuerza e ingenio con la que construye su casita. Unimos ciencias, informática y desarrollo técnico con raíces profundamente santiagueñas, demostrando con orgullo el poder de nuestra creatividad, imaginación y talento para llevar la innovación de nuestra provincia a lo más alto.
summary: FAVALORO (Flight Assessment of Vitals, Ambient Loads, and Operational Readiness Oversight) is a web-based health monitoring system for astronauts on long-duration missions, built for the moments when Earth cannot answer in time. We developed a low-cost wristband based on an ESP32 that measures heart rate, blood oxygen, and temperature over standard Bluetooth, with no action required from the astronaut. A voice companion, powered by an open-source AI that runs offline in the browser, talks with the crew member and fills in what no sensor can measure: mood, stress, perceived sleep, and meals. The app offers four role-based views (crew member, medical officer, commander, and mission specialist). If an emergency call goes unanswered for 30 seconds, it escalates automatically to the nearest crewmate, the physician, and Mission Control. Its limits and rules are based on NASA-STD-3001, the five Human Research Program hazards, and MEDB data. This matters because, with up to 24 minutes of delay from Mars, astronauts must detect health changes on their own. FAVALORO measures, converses, prevents, and acts autonomously.
details:
What it does and how it works. FAVALORO is a single web app (HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, no frameworks or installation) that works as an integrated health and environment monitor. A custom wristband (ESP32 + MAX30102 for pulse and SpO₂ + MLX90614 for contactless temperature) publishes the standard Bluetooth health services (heart rate 0x180D, pulse oximeter 0x1822, thermometer 0x1809), so the app also accepts compatible commercial devices via Web Bluetooth. Metrics the wristband cannot capture are collected by a voice companion that asks the remaining questions of the 14-item mind and stress check, plus nutrition and mood, using the browser’s Web Speech API. The wristband already answers 3 of those 14 questions (sleep hours, awakenings, resting pulse), so they are never asked.

The app has four views: crew member (daily log, sleep stages, tests, family and diary, nutrition), medical officer (clinical file, adapted NEWS2 early warning, medicine cabinet, Earth consultation with real delays, NASA evaluation plan), commander (daily report, fitness for tasks such as spacewalks, decisions, emergencies), and mission specialist (cabin environment, life support, solar radiation, the five hazards). The environment can be switched between Space Station, Moon base, and Mars habitat.

Benefits and impact. Astronauts spend less time on questionnaires, get early detection of changes, and receive guided help even with no connection to Earth. Automatic escalation (alarm, nearest crewmate, physician, Mission Control) removes the dependence on a delayed response. Each role sees only what it needs, and private diary entries are never shared. The same approach could serve Antarctic bases, offshore platforms, and remote rural areas.

Tools used. HTML/CSS/JavaScript, WebLLM (Qwen 2.5 / Llama 3.2 running on WebGPU), Web Bluetooth, Web Speech API, Web Audio, localStorage and IndexedDB, Lenis, Python server, Cloudflare Tunnel and GitHub Pages, ESP32 with SparkFun MAX3010x and Adafruit MLX90614 libraries. Claude (Anthropic) assisted with code, presentation videos, and logo design.

Creativity. A voice companion that fills in the forms for the astronaut, a custom wristband built on open standards, and an offline open-source AI with automatic escalation to Mission Control.

Factors considered. NASA-STD-3001, the five HRP hazards, MEDB documents, and OCHMO technical briefs; accessibility (WCAG 2.1 AA, high contrast, large text, 44 px touch targets); privacy; and low cost. Crew data is currently simulated, FAVALORO is not a medical device, and the demo thresholds still need validation with physicians.
